newsitem.title: USA: Steller's eider declared a threatened species.
newsitem.headline: Steller's eider declared a threatened species.

text.p: The population of Alaska-breeding Steller's eiders was declared a threatened species on Wednesday by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

The small ducks, which used to nest along the coastline from southwestern Alaska's Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta to the Canadian border in northeastern Alaska, are now found in only a tiny part of their former breeding grounds, the Fish and Wildlife Service said.

"By listing the species under the Endangered Species Act, attention will be focused on the species' conservation. We expect that future conservation efforts will also benefit other sea ducks that occur in Alaska," David Allen, Fish and Wildlife Service director for Alaska, said in a news release.

Of the estimated 140,000 Steller's eiders worldwide, only a few hundred pairs of the birds are believed to live in Alaska, agency spokeswoman Connie Barclay said. Only a few dozen pairs of the birds are spotted in Alaska each year, she said.

Most of the birds' world population is in Russia , Barclay said. The Alaska population breeds along a defined stretch of the North Slope coastline, mostly near Barrow, the northernmost point in the United States, she said.
In the past two decades, only two Steller's eider nests have been found in North America, Barclay said.
The reason for the eiders' decline is unclear, she said. The biologists don't know," Barclay said. "It's a total mystery as to what's happened."
Some theories blame lead shot -- which used to be used by hunters and which is toxic to birds -- habitat contamination or ecosystem changes in the Bering Sea, Barclay said.

The Steller's eider, named for German naturalist Georg Steller, is the smallest of the four eider species. The males have distinctive black eye patches on their white heads, the Fish and Wildlife Service said.
During the winter, the diving ducks inhabit shallow waters long the Alaska Peninsula and eastern Aleutian Islands in Alaska but move inland for the breeding season, the agency said.
